title: Short Stuff: Centralia Coal Fire
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Centralia coal fire, the underground coal seam fire burning beneath the small former mining town of Centralia, Pennsylvania since 1962. The hosts cover how coal seam fires start and spread (including abandoned mines, spontaneous combustion of anthracite, and fires elsewhere such as China, India, and Burning Mountain in Australia), the competing origin stories (a deliberate landfill burn, a garbage fire started by a truck driver, or a smoldering fire first noticed in the 1960s), the town's dwindling population of about ten residents, the relocation efforts, the 2002 zip code removal, the closure of Route 61, the early-1980s street collapse, and failed attempts to extinguish the fire such as vent pipes and trenching.

segments.title: Opening banter and Centralia introduction
segments.summary: Hosts open the short episode and introduce Centralia, Pennsylvania, a small former mining town where an underground coal fire has burned for decades and only about ten residents remain.

segments.title: What a coal seam fire is
segments.summary: Coal seams are natural underground coal deposits that can burn for long periods. Coal seam fires are common worldwide, with examples in China and in India's Jharia coal field, and abandoned mines that are not properly sealed can make them worse.

segments.title: Spontaneous combustion and cellular foam
segments.summary: Coal can self-heat through oxidation and spontaneously ignite, especially anthracite, making coal shipments dangerous. A company's cellular foam made of Portland cement and fly ash can be sprayed on leftover coal to prevent fires.

segments.title: Origin theories of the Centralia fire
segments.summary: The most popular account says the fire began in 1962 when a landfill was burned on purpose and the flames reached a coal seam. Other accounts blame a garbage fire started by a truck driver, or say the fire smoldered from the 1930s and was only noticed in the 1960s. The fire spreads through tunnels roughly 100 to 300 feet below ground and is still burning, with steam visible on rainy days.

segments.title: Relocation, road closure, and the town's decline
segments.summary: About ten residents remain by choice. Pennsylvania's government removed Centralia's zip code in 2002 and closed part of Route 61. In the early 1980s a boy's fall into a collapsed street prompted the relocation effort, and the town has since demolished buildings. Accounts of the incident differ.

segments.title: Attempts to extinguish the fire
segments.summary: Efforts included vent pipes in the 1980s, which were later sealed because they fed the fire oxygen, and a trench meant as a firebreak that the fire outran. Such fires are hard to extinguish and need constant monitoring. Burning Mountain in New South Wales, Australia, has reportedly burned for about 6,000 years.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close the episode and give the standard Stuff You Should Know sign-off.
